rationale: A wins because it gives the founder four genuinely different reporting lanes: scale, policy/access, study scrutiny, and money. Its "What Calm actually gets paid when 25 million people get it for free" is the useful business angle B wrongly throws away, while B's "The Wellness-to-Clinical Shift Is Arriving" dresses one partnership up as a category coronation. A has one loaded line, "instead of paying for real anxiety care," but it at least asks for the missing proof instead of pretending the proof exists.
gaps_in_A: "default benefit" overstates the fact pattern. The update says Calm Premium is a covered no-cost benefit; it does not say automatic enrollment, default plan placement, or opt-out status.
"instead of paying for real anxiety care" is a sharp question, but it is loaded beyond the evidence. The facts do not show insurers are substituting Calm for therapy or psychiatric care.
"tests whether app-based \"wellness\" benefits satisfy parity obligations" leans on a legal/policy frame before the plan-design facts exist. Keep it as a reporting question, not a premise.
gaps_in_B: "The Wellness-to-Clinical Shift Is Arriving" is category-theater. One Calm deal plus one Calm-funded study does not prove an industry shift.
"Coverage Was the Last Wall" is unsupported. The update gives coverage scale, not evidence that coverage was the final barrier to mental-health access or app adoption.

"The prevailing belief in tech-health press is that independent university execution neutralizes industry funding" invents a straw man. The conflict angle is valid without manufacturing a belief system for the beat.
"Business/revenue mechanics — no_journalist_shape" is flatly wrong. "No revenue terms disclosed" is exactly why a digital-health business reporter may chase the payment model.
